title: Design a Distributed Cache
tagline: Build a Redis-style cache cluster that is fast, grows by adding nodes and never takes the database down with it.

statement.prompt: Design a **distributed in-memory cache** (like a Redis or Memcached cluster) that many application servers share to avoid slow database reads.
context: You are in a 45-minute interview. The interviewer wants more than 'use Redis'.
Your applications already have a relational database that is the source of truth.
The cache must keep working as machines are added, removed or crash.
given: About **200 million** items matter; roughly **20% are hot**.
Hundreds of thousands of operations per second.

expectations.title: Drive the conversation
expectations.body: Ask questions before drawing anything. State your assumptions out loud so they can be corrected early.

expectations.title: Use numbers
expectations.body: Turn the givens into requests per second, storage and bandwidth. Every later choice should point back to one of them.

expectations.title: Start simple, then evolve
expectations.body: Get a working version on the board first. Add caches, sharding and queues only when a number or a requirement asks for them.

expectations.title: Go deep on the hard parts
expectations.body: For this problem the hard parts are choosing the placement scheme, keeping the cache and database consistent, and surviving node loss without flooding the database.

expectations.title: Name the trade-offs
expectations.body: Say what you chose, what you gave up, and what would make you change your mind.

expectations.title: Think about failure
expectations.body: Point out single points of failure and say what happens when a node, a cache or a whole zone goes down.

scope_in: Failure modes like stampede and hot keys
great: Explains **LRU in O(1)** with a hash map and linked list.
Names **stampede, penetration, avalanche and hot key** with a fix for each.
Deletes on write and keeps the **database the source of truth**.

concepts.def: Least Recently Used: evict the entry that has not been touched for the longest time.
Time to live: after this long the entry expires.
The application checks the cache, and on a miss reads the database and fills the cache.
Many requests miss on the same key and all hit the database at once.
One key getting so much traffic that a single node cannot cope.

numbers: 200M x 20% x 1 KB = about **40 GB** hot data
Memory access is roughly **100 ns**; a network hop to a cache is about **0.5 ms**; a database query is **5 to 50 ms**

takeaways: Single node: **hash map + doubly linked list** gives O(1) LRU.
Shard with **consistent hashing**; replicate shards for availability.
Defend against **stampede, penetration, avalanche and hot keys** so the database is safe.

tradeoffs.cost: App code owns the logic; first read is slow
Lower hit rate, more DB load

extensions: Near-cache in each app for the hottest keys

steps.title: What does the cache do?
steps.prompt: Which operations belong in the scope of a distributed cache?
steps.hint: Is it the source of truth?
steps.explain: A distributed cache is **fast, shared, and disposable**: losing a key costs a database read, not data.

notes: API: get, set with TTL, delete; eviction; add/remove nodes online

options.text: Evict entries when memory is full
options.why: Memory is finite.

options.text: `delete(key)`
options.why: Invalidate on change.

options.text: `get(key)`
options.why: Read.

options.text: Add and remove cache nodes while running
options.why: Scale and failures without an outage.

options.text: Guaranteed durable storage of every key
options.why: A cache can lose data. The database is the source of truth.

options.text: `set(key, value, ttl)`
options.why: Write with an expiry.

steps.title: What qualities matter?
steps.prompt: Pick the requirements that shape the design.
steps.hint: What does the app team expect from it?
steps.explain: **Speed, throughput, availability, scalability.** Consistency with the database is *eventual*, managed with TTLs and deletes.

notes: Qualities: ~1 ms, very high throughput, highly available, scalable; eventually consistent with the DB

options.text: High throughput (hundreds of thousands of ops/s)
options.why: Thousands of app servers share it.

options.text: High availability: a node loss must not melt the database
options.why: The key reliability concern.

options.text: Strong consistency with the database at all times
options.why: Costly. Accept small staleness with TTL and invalidation.

options.text: Latency around 1 ms
options.why: The reason caches exist.

options.text: Scalability: grow memory by adding nodes
options.why: Horizontal growth.

steps.title: How much memory?
steps.prompt: Your service has **200 million** items that matter. About **20%** are hot enough to cache. Each cached item is **1 KB**. How many **GB** of cache memory?
steps.hint: Items times the hot share times item size.
steps.explain: About **40 GB of data, ~100 GB provisioned**. That is a handful of ordinary cache nodes (32 to 64 GB each). It shows why memory, not disk, is the resource you size.

notes: Capacity: ~40 GB hot data, ~100 GB provisioned with overhead and replicas

work: Add overhead (about 30-50% for keys and bookkeeping) and replication: plan for **100 GB or more** across the cluster

steps.title: One machine first
steps.prompt: Inside one node you need `get` and `set` in O(1) with LRU eviction. Which structure?
steps.hint: You need fast lookup AND fast reordering.
steps.explain: **Hash map + doubly linked list = LRU in O(1).** In Python an `OrderedDict` gives you this directly.

notes: Single node: hash map + doubly linked list (LRU, O(1))

options.text: An array scanned for the key
options.why: O(n) lookups.

options.text: A queue only
options.why: You cannot find a key in the middle quickly.

options.text: A hash map plus a doubly linked list (the map points to list nodes; touch moves a node to the front, evict from the tail)
options.why: Both lookup and reorder are O(1).

options.text: A sorted tree keyed by last-used time
options.why: O(log n) and heavier than needed.

steps.title: Spreading keys across nodes
steps.prompt: How should keys be assigned to cache nodes?
steps.hint: What happens to the keys when N changes?
steps.explain: **Consistent hashing** is what makes online scaling cheap. With modulo placement, adding one node effectively empties the cache.

notes: Placement: consistent hashing with virtual nodes in the client library

options.text: Each app server keeps its own private cache
options.why: Duplicates data, low hit rate, inconsistent.

options.text: Send every request to every node
options.why: Wasteful.

options.text: `hash(key) % N`
options.why: Change N and almost every key remaps: a mass cache miss that floods the database.

options.text: Consistent hashing in the client library (or a proxy), with virtual nodes
options.why: Adding or removing a node remaps only a small fraction of keys.

steps.title: The read path
steps.prompt: Order a read that **misses** the cache under cache-aside.
steps.explain: **Cache-aside**: the app owns the logic and the cache is dumb storage. Simple and robust, and the pattern you can defend in any interview.

items.text: The app hashes the key and picks the cache node
The cache node reports a miss
The app writes the value to the cache with a TTL
The app returns the value to the caller
items.why: Cache fill is not on the critical path for correctness.

steps.title: Writes and invalidation
steps.prompt: A user updates their profile in the database. What should happen to the cached copy?
steps.explain: **Write the database, then delete the cache key.** Short TTLs are the safety net for anything that goes wrong.

notes: Writes: update the database, then delete the cache key; TTL as safety net

steps.followup: What race can still leave stale data after delete-on-write?

options.text: Delete the cache entry after the database write (the next read repopulates it)
options.why: Simple and avoids races of writing two places.

options.text: Write to both with no ordering care
options.why: Concurrent writers can leave the cache holding the older value.

options.text: Do nothing and wait for the TTL
options.why: Users see their old profile for minutes.

options.text: Update the cache first, then the database
options.why: If the database write fails, the cache holds data that never existed.

steps.title: Cache disasters
steps.prompt: Match the problem to its defence. Select the **correct** defences.
steps.hint: Same data hit again and again, or all at once.
steps.explain: Name the four: **stampede, penetration, avalanche, hot key.** Each has a cheap defence.

notes: Defences: request coalescing, cache negatives, TTL jitter, local cache for hot keys

options.text: All of these are rare, ignore them
options.why: They cause real outages.

options.text: Penetration by non-existent keys: cache the 'not found' for a short time or use a Bloom filter
options.why: Stops repeated useless database hits.

options.text: Hot key overload: a small local in-process cache or replicas of that key
options.why: One key can overload one node.

options.text: Stampede on a hot expired key: request coalescing (one rebuilds, others wait) or refresh-ahead
options.why: Avoids thousands of identical database reads.

options.text: Avalanche from simultaneous expiry: add random jitter to TTLs
options.why: Spreads expiry over time.

steps.title: A cache node dies
steps.prompt: What keeps the database alive when a node disappears?
steps.hint: Cache failure is a database problem in disguise.
steps.explain: Plan the **blast radius**: replicas, small remap, protected database, warm replacements.

notes: HA: replicas per shard, small remap, DB protection, warm replacements

options.text: Rate limiting and coalescing on the database path
options.why: Protects the database from the miss wave.

options.text: Let every request retry immediately until it works
options.why: Retry storms melt the database.

options.text: Replicas of each shard, promoted on failure
options.why: Most keys survive.

options.text: Pre-warming a replacement node before it takes traffic
options.why: A cold node means a miss storm.

options.text: Consistent hashing so only that node's share of keys is remapped
options.why: A small, not total, miss wave.

steps.title: Which eviction policy?
steps.prompt: Memory is full. Which policy is the sensible default, and when would you change it?
steps.explain: **LRU by default**; mention that real systems approximate it (sample a few keys, evict the oldest) because tracking exact order is costly.

notes: Eviction: LRU default (approximate in practice), LFU for stable popularity

options.text: FIFO always
options.why: Evicts the oldest even if it is hot.

options.text: LRU by default; LFU for stable popularity; TTL-based for time-bound data
options.why: Pick by access pattern.

options.text: Random always
options.why: Fine as a cheap approximation (Redis samples randomly), but not a design principle.

options.text: Never evict, reject writes
options.why: The cache becomes useless when full.

steps.title: Defend your design
steps.prompt: In two or three sentences: what does a distributed cache trade away?
steps.explain: Close by repeating **"the database stays the source of truth"**.

notes: Trade-offs: staleness vs speed; cache outage risk; async replication may lose recent writes

steps.model: A cache trades **consistency and simplicity** for **speed and database relief**. Data can be briefly stale (TTL and delete-on-write narrow the gap), there is a whole new failure mode (cache outage hitting the database), and extra operational work (sizing, eviction, hot keys). Asynchronous replication means a failover can lose a few recent entries, which is acceptable because the cache is never the source of truth.
points: New failure mode: stampede onto the database
Async replication may lose recent entries
Cache is never the source of truth
